introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education (GCE) Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Philosophy 2 (0790), Paper 2 (Philosophical Culture), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Duration: three hours.**

Candidates are required to answer FOUR (04) questions, chosen from the three Sections imperatively.

Each essay question shall be marked according to the following criteria:
- An introduction: 5 marks
- A thesis: 7 marks
- An antithesis: 6 marks
- A synthesis: 3 marks
- A conclusion: 4 marks

Each question carries 25 marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : la page de garde dit « answer FOUR (04) questions, chosen from the three Sections imperatively » (quatre questions au total, prises dans les trois sections, donc au moins une par section). `regles_choix` porte le minimum, une règle `parmi 1 sur 2` par section (Section One : questions 1-2 ; Section Two : questions 3-4 ; Section Three : questions 5-6) ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`. Le sujet imprime « Sub Section Two: Text on African Philosophy » au-dessus de la question 6 mais aucun intitulé « Sub Section One » au-dessus de la question 5 (texte de Descartes) : la Section Three est comptée comme une seule section de deux questions ; le sujet ne dit pas si un candidat peut traiter les questions 5 et 6 à la fois.

Points : chaque question est imprimée « 25 marks » (4 x 25 = 100). Les critères de la page de garde (introduction 5, thèse 7, antithèse 6, synthèse 3, conclusion 4 = 25) s'appliquent aux dissertations (questions 1 à 4) ; les questions de textes (5 et 6) ont leurs points par sous-question (5 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 25 pour chacune) : aucun écart de somme constaté, aucun point corrigé.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans accès à une source. Les auteurs et positions cités sont ceux de l'histoire de la philosophie établie, sans citation littérale, sans numéro de page et sans date hormis des repères généraux sûrs ; à faire relire par un enseignant de philosophie avant mise en avant.

Sujet scanné (3 pages) avec filigrane gcerevision.com sans incidence sur la lecture ; aucune figure. Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, Philosophy 2, Paper 2 (Philosophical Culture), code 0790, JUNE 2022, trois heures.

Q3 : positions attribuées à Senghor (négritude comme ensemble des valeurs culturelles du monde noir, formule « l'émotion est nègre comme la raison est hellène », civilisation de l'universel), à Césaire (invention du mot), à Sartre (« racisme antiraciste », sans titre d'ouvrage), à Towa (critique de la négritude, appel à la maîtrise de la raison, de la science et de la technique), à Soyinka (formule du tigre, rapportée avec la prudence « widely credited ») et à Fanon : grandes lignes sûres, aucune citation littérale, aucun titre d'ouvrage, aucune date hormis les repères généraux. Les noms propres sont écrits sans accents dans le corrigé (Aime Cesaire, Leon-Gontran Damas, Leopold Sedar Senghor).

questions.enonce_markdown:
"Negritude was a rallying point and part of a language of resistance to the stereotype of Black African People". Is this fair assessment of Senghor's Negritude?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction (5 marks).** Negritude is the movement of black affirmation born among black students in Paris in the 1930s around Aime Cesaire, Leon-Gontran Damas and Leopold Sedar Senghor (1906-2001), later the first President of Senegal. Cesaire is credited with the word; Senghor made it a philosophy of the black world, which he defined broadly as the sum of the cultural values of the black peoples. The statement to be assessed says that Negritude was "a rallying point and part of a language of resistance to the stereotype of Black African people". The problem is whether this is a fair description of Senghor's Negritude, or whether it leaves out its limits and its more doctrinal side.

**Thesis: the assessment is fair (7 marks).**
- *Historical context.* Colonial ideology, and a long Western tradition of racial thought, presented Africans as people without history, reason or civilisation, who were to be "civilised". Negritude was born as a refusal of assimilation, which asked the colonised to abandon their identity in order to become "Frenchmen".
- *A rallying point.* Negritude gave black intellectuals from Africa and the Caribbean a common name, a shared pride and a community of purpose. The term turned a word of contempt into a word of dignity. Its reviews and its literature (poetry, essays, later the journal Presence Africaine) brought together people separated by colonial borders.
- *A language of resistance.* Senghor insisted on the originality of African civilisation: its sense of rhythm, its communion with nature, its symbolic and artistic vision of the world, its community values. His much-quoted contrast, that emotion is black as reason is Greek, was meant to affirm a different way of knowing, not to claim inferiority. By rehabilitating African art and culture he contested the stereotype of the "savage", and he argued for a "civilisation of the universal" to which each culture contributes (the "rendez-vous of giving and receiving").
- Negritude also fed the cultural side of the independence movements and later African literature.

**Antithesis: the assessment is incomplete (6 marks).**
- *It adopts the stereotype it fights.* Critics argue that by opposing black emotion to white reason Senghor kept the colonial categories and only reversed their value. Sartre, in an essay introducing a collection of Negritude poetry, called it an "anti-racist racism" and a necessary moment in a dialectic that should lead beyond race.
- *Essentialism.* To speak of one "black soul" or one "African mind" ignores the diversity of African peoples and societies, and overlooks classes, history and change. Marcien Towa, a Cameroonian philosopher, criticised Senghor's Negritude as a form of cultural dependence that did not equip Africans to master the modern world; he urged critical self-assertion and the mastery of science and technology.
- *Backward-looking and politically limited.* Wole Soyinka is widely credited with the remark that a tiger does not proclaim its tigritude, it pounces, meaning that freedom is shown in action, not in talk about one's essence. Frantz Fanon and others held that Negritude was a necessary stage but that the struggle for liberation had to be political and economic. Senghor's own later politics (close relations with France and a gradual path) led some to see it as an ideology of the elite.

**Synthesis (3 marks).** The assessment is accurate as a description of the historical function of Negritude: it was a rallying point and a language of resistance to a demeaning image. It is not a complete assessment of Senghor's thought, which goes beyond resistance to a positive theory of African culture and of cultural exchange, and which has been criticised for that very theory.

**Conclusion (4 marks).** The statement is fair as far as it goes. Negritude restored dignity, gave a common voice to black people and stood against colonial stereotypes. But the word "resistance" must not hide its limits: its essentialism, its closeness to the categories it opposed, and its weakness as a programme of political and economic liberation. It is best seen as a necessary first moment of African self-affirmation, to be developed by more critical and practical forms of thought.
